question: In public health, what do we mean by 'food supply'?

options.A: The exact number of calories a single person eats daily
options.B: The specific diet chosen by individual families at home
options.C: The total amount of food produced and made available in a region
options.D: The amount of money budgeted for grocery shopping

explanation: Food supply is simply about the total food available through farming, storage, and trade across a whole area. You've got this! [learn more](GNS227_U2_T027#GNS227_U2_T027_h1)

question: Why doesn't having plenty of food in the country automatically mean everyone is well-nourished?

options.A: Government regulations legally restrict citizens from buying more than basic rations
options.B: Local populations automatically reject imported food items due to personal preferences
options.C: Stored food spoils instantly before it can be transported to local neighborhood markets
options.D: Food may be present in the country but remain unaffordable or inaccessible to poor households

explanation: Just because food is in the country doesn't mean poor families have the money to buy it. Distribution and wealth play huge roles! [learn more](GNS227_U2_T027#GNS227_U2_T027_h1)

question: What is a major reason farm crops get wasted before they ever reach the market?

options.A: Excessive consumer demand in local supermarkets
options.B: Poor storage facilities and inadequate transport networks
options.C: Immediate consumption of all crops by farmers
options.D: Strict government laws against selling fresh crops

explanation: Bad roads and lack of proper storage silos mean harvested food often spoils before getting to people who need it. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T027#GNS227_U2_T027_h2)

question: If a country relies heavily on importing most of its food, what is the biggest risk to its food supply?

options.A: Local soil becoming too fertile to grow native food crops
options.B: Farmers in the home country producing too much surplus grain locally
options.C: Global shipping disruptions and sudden price spikes on international markets
options.D: Citizens losing their appetite for imported grain products over time

explanation: When you depend on other nations for food, any global shipping crisis or sudden price jump hits your country hard. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T027#GNS227_U2_T027_h2)

question: When food prices shoot up due to inflation, how do many families change what they eat?

options.A: They grow all their missing food requirements in backyard container gardens
options.B: They substitute nutrient-dense foods with cheaper, calorie-dense refined carbohydrates
options.C: They automatically increase their daily intake of fresh fruits and lean meats
options.D: They stop eating entirely until government food subsidies arrive in the mail

explanation: When money gets tight, families swap out expensive veggies and proteins for cheaper filler foods that fill the belly but lack vitamins. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T027#GNS227_U2_T027_h3)

question: If local stores see a drop in meat sales and a huge spike in cheap instant noodles, what does this usually tell us?

options.A: Improved local agricultural output of grain-based factory foods
options.B: An unexpected surplus of manufacturing capacity for wheat products
options.C: A sudden cultural shift favoring processed instant meals over cooking
options.D: Decreased household purchasing power altering dietary choices

explanation: When people have less money, they buy cheaper comfort foods, changing their overall diet quality. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T027#GNS227_U2_T027_h3)

question: What exactly is a 'food desert'?

options.A: An area with limited access to affordable and nutritious fresh food sources
options.B: A government zone where farming is legally banned to protect wildlife
options.C: A marketplace that sells only imported canned goods and bottled water
options.D: A barren desert region where no plant life or agriculture can survive

explanation: A food desert is a neighborhood lacking nearby fresh food markets, leaving residents with poor nutritional options. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T027#GNS227_U2_T027_h4)

question: Why might a rural village suddenly see vitamin deficiencies during the heavy rainy season?

options.A: Excessive rainfall causing an overabundance of fresh meat in local stores
options.B: Villagers deliberately choosing to fast from fruits and vegetables during rainstorms
options.C: Washed-out roads cutting off transport of fresh produce from regional markets
options.D: Soil contamination making all locally grown crops completely poisonous

explanation: Bad weather washes out roads, isolating communities so fresh, perishable foods can't get delivered. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T027#GNS227_U2_T027_h4)

question: Why do nurses need to keep cultural and religious beliefs in mind when giving diet advice?

options.A: Because cultural beliefs completely override all biological needs for protein
options.B: Because hospital regulations require patients to follow traditional holiday menus
options.C: Because religious leaders must personally approve every prescribed hospital meal
options.D: Because food consumption habits are deeply tied to tradition, identity, and social norms

explanation: Food is tied to who we are. If you ignore cultural traditions, patients simply won't follow your nutrition advice. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T027#GNS227_U2_T027_h5)

question: Nursing mothers refuse to eat iron-rich organ meats because of a local cultural taboo. What is the best first step for a nurse?

options.A: Identify alternative culturally accepted foods that provide similar iron content
options.B: Tell the mothers their cultural beliefs are completely wrong and unscientific
options.C: Report the mothers to hospital authorities for refusing standard medical advice
options.D: Force-feed the organ meats to ensure the mothers meet daily iron targets

explanation: Great nursing is about teamwork! Instead of fighting tradition, help them find other foods they *are* allowed to eat that give them the same iron. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T027#GNS227_U2_T027_h5)

question: What is the main meaning of 'food insecurity'?

options.A: Temporary fasting practiced during religious or cultural holiday seasons
options.B: A personal choice to go on a strict weight-loss diet for health reasons
options.C: Lack of consistent access to enough safe and nutritious food for a healthy life
options.D: Having too many grocery stores in a single neighborhood community

explanation: Food insecurity means a person or family never quite knows where their next wholesome meal is coming from. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T027#GNS227_U2_T027_h6)

question: Which of these is NOT a normal health result of long-term household food insecurity?

options.A: Micronutrient deficiencies like anemia and scurvy
options.B: Childhood physical stunting and developmental delay
options.C: Obesity linked to cheap, high-calorie processed foods

explanation: Food insecurity causes malnutrition, stunting, or poor diet-related health—never peak athletic fitness! [learn more](GNS227_U2_T027#GNS227_U2_T027_h6)

question: Why do governments mandate food fortification, like adding iodine to table salt?

options.A: To change the natural color and taste of everyday grocery products
options.B: To prevent common micronutrient deficiency diseases across the population
options.C: To artificially increase the commercial market price of basic food items
options.D: To reduce the total number of calories found in packaged goods

explanation: Fortifying everyday foods helps protect the whole community from sneaky vitamin and mineral deficiencies. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T027#GNS227_U2_T027_h7)

question: During a clinic visit, you suspect a mother cannot afford enough healthy food for her kids. What should you do?

options.A: Screen for food insecurity and connect the family with local food assistance programs
options.B: Assume the children are eating well because they do not look underweight
options.C: Prescribe expensive daily vitamin supplements without checking family resources
options.D: Advise the mother to spend less money on household electricity and clothing

explanation: Always look out for your patients' social needs! Connecting struggling families to support programs makes a real difference. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T027#GNS227_U2_T027_h7)
